happy-life_section-19.plainEnglish: You say that no one lives up to their own words or follows the high standards they preach about. What do you expect? Their words are brave and grand — big enough to survive any storm that destroys people. But they themselves are struggling to escape the crosses they've nailed themselves to. At least criminals on crosses hang from just one pole. But these self-punishing people are stretched across as many crosses as they have desires. And yet they still badmouth others. They act so superior when judging other people's flaws that you'd think they had none of their own — if it weren't for the fact that some criminals actually spit on their audience from the gallows.

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
"Philosophers do not carry into effect all that they teach."
No; but they effect much good by their teaching, by the noble
thoughts which they conceive in their minds: would, indeed, that
they could act up to their talk: what could be happier than they
would be? but in the meanwhile you have no right to despise good
sayings and hearts full of good thoughts. Men deserve praise for
engaging in profitable studies, even though they stop short of
producing any results. Why need we wonder if those who begin to
climb a steep path do not succeed in ascending it very high? yet,
if you be a man, look with respect on those who attempt great things,
even though they fall. It is the act of a generous spirit to
proportion its efforts not to its own strength but to that of human
nature, to entertain lofty aims, and to conceive plans which are
too vast to be carried into execution even by those who are endowed
with gigantic intellects, who appoint for themselves the following
rules:
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish:
"Philosophers don't practice what they preach."

No, but they do a lot of good through their teaching. They create noble ideas in their minds. I wish they could live up to their words perfectly — what could be happier than that? But you still have no right to dismiss good ideas and hearts full of good thoughts. People deserve praise for studying valuable things, even if they don't achieve perfect results. Why should we be surprised when people trying to climb a steep mountain don't make it to the very top? But if you're human, show respect for those who attempt great things, even when they fail. It shows a generous spirit to aim your efforts not just at what you can handle, but at what human nature itself can reach for. To have lofty goals and make plans too big to complete — even for people with giant minds — who set themselves these rules:

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
I will look upon death or upon a comedy with the same
expression of countenance: I will submit to labours, however great
they may be, supporting the strength of my body by that of
my mind: I will despise riches when I have them as much as when I
have them not; if they be elsewhere I will not be more gloomy, if
they sparkle around me I will not be more lively than I should
otherwise be: whether Fortune comes or goes I will take no notice
of her: I will view all lands as though they belong to me, and my
own as though they belonged to all mankind: I will so live as to
remember that I was born for others, and will thank Nature on this
account: for in what fashion could she have done better for me? she
has given me alone to all, and all to me alone. Whatever I may
possess, I will neither hoard it greedily nor squander it recklessly.
I will think that I have no possessions so real as those which I
have given away to deserving people: I will not reckon benefits by
their magnitude or number, or by anything except the value set upon
them by the receiver: I never will consider a gift to be a large
one if it be bestowed upon a worthy object. I will do nothing because
of public opinion, but everything because of conscience:
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish: I will face death or watch a comedy with the same calm expression. I will take on any hard work, no matter how difficult, using my mind to strengthen my body. I will care as little about riches when I have them as when I don't. If money is somewhere else, I won't be gloomy. If it surrounds me, I won't be more excited than I should be. Whether Fortune comes or goes, I won't even notice her. I will see all lands as if they belong to me, and my own land as if it belongs to everyone. I will live remembering that I was born to help others, and I will thank Nature for this. How could she have done better for me? She has given me alone to everyone, and everyone to me alone. Whatever I own, I won't hoard it greedily or waste it carelessly. I will think my only real possessions are the things I have given away to people who deserve them. I won't judge my good deeds by how big they are or how many I do, but only by how much they mean to the person who receives them. I will never think a gift is too small if it goes to someone worthy.

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
whenever
I do anything alone by myself I will believe that the eyes of the
Roman people are upon me while I do it. In eating and drinking my
object shall be to quench the desires of Nature, not to fill and
empty my belly. I will be agreeable with my friends, gentle and
mild to my foes: I will grant pardon before I am asked for it, and
will meet the wishes of honourable men half way: I will bear in
mind that the world is my native city, that its governors are the
gods, and that they stand above and around me, criticizing whatever
I do or say. Whenever either Nature demands my breath again, or
reason bids me dismiss it, I will quit this life, calling all to
witness that I have loved a good conscience, and good pursuits;
that no one's freedom, my own least of all, has been impaired through
me." He who sets up these as the rules of his life will soar aloft
and strive to make his way to the gods: of a truth, even though he
fails, yet he

"Fails in a high emprise."[4]
happy-life_section-20.plainEnglish: I will do nothing because of public opinion, but everything because of conscience. Whenever I do anything alone, I will imagine that all the Roman people are watching me. When I eat and drink, my goal will be to satisfy nature's needs, not to stuff and empty my belly. I will be pleasant with my friends and gentle with my enemies. I will forgive before I'm even asked, and I will meet good people halfway. I will remember that the world is my home city, that the gods are its rulers, and that they stand above and around me, judging everything I do or say. When nature demands my last breath, or when reason tells me it's time to go, I will leave this life. And I will call everyone to witness that I have loved a good conscience and good pursuits — that no one's freedom, especially my own, has been damaged because of me. The person who makes these the rules of his life will soar high and strive to reach the gods. Even if he fails, he

happy-life_section-20.originalText:
But you, who hate both virtue and those who practise it, do nothing
at which we need be surprised, for sickly lights cannot bear the
sun, nocturnal creatures avoid the brightness of day, and at its
first dawning become bewildered and all betake themselves to their
dens together: creatures that fear the light hide themselves in
crevices. So croak away, and exercise your miserable tongues in
reproaching good men: open wide your jaws, bite hard: you will break
many teeth before you make any impression.

happy-life_section-21.originalText: "But how is it that this man studies philosophy and nevertheless lives the life of a rich man? Why does he say that wealth ought to be despised and yet possess it? that life should be despised, and yet live? that health should be despised, and yet guard it with the utmost care, and wish it to be as good as possible? Does he consider banishment to be an empty name, and say, "What evil is there in changing one country for another?" and yet, if permitted, does he not grow old in his native land? does he declare that there is no difference between a longer and a shorter time, and yet, if he be not prevented, lengthen out his life and flourish in a green old age?" His answer is, that these things ought to be despised, not that he should not possess them, but that he should not possess them with fear and trembling: he does not drive them away from him, but when they leave him he follows after them unconcernedly. Where, indeed, can fortune invest riches more securely than in a place from whence they can always be recovered without any squabble with their trustee?
happy-life_section-21.plainEnglish: But how can this man study philosophy and still live like a rich person? Why does he say wealth should be despised but keep his money? Why say life should be despised but go on living? Why say health doesn't matter but take the best care of his body and want to stay as healthy as possible? He calls exile just an empty word and asks, "What's so bad about moving from one country to another?" Yet if he's allowed, doesn't he prefer to grow old in his homeland? He says there's no difference between a long life and a short one, yet if nothing stops him, doesn't he try to live as long as possible and enjoy a healthy old age? His answer is this: these things should be despised, but that doesn't mean he can't have them. It means he shouldn't cling to them in fear. He doesn't push them away, but when they leave him, he doesn't chase after them frantically. Really, where could fortune store riches more safely than with someone who can always give them back without fighting their keeper?

happy-life_section-21.originalText: Marcus Cato, when he was praising Curius and Coruncanius and that century in which the possession of a few small silver coins were an offence which was punished by the Censor, himself owned four million sesterces; a less fortune no doubt, than that of Crassus, but larger than of Cato the Censor. If the amounts be compared, he had outstripped his great-grandfather further than he himself was outdone by Crassus, and if still greater riches had fallen to his lot, he would not have spurned them: for the wise man does not think himself unworthy of any chance presents: he does not love riches, but he prefers to have them; he does not receive them into his spirit, but only into his house: nor does he cast away from him what he already possesses, but keeps them, and is willing that his virtue should receive a larger subject-matter for its exercise.
happy-life_section-21.plainEnglish: Marcus Cato used to praise Curius and Coruncanius and their generation — a time when owning a few silver coins was considered corrupt and the Censors would punish you for it. Yet Cato himself owned four million sesterces. That was less than Crassus had, but much more than his great-grandfather Cato the Censor ever owned. Compared to his ancestor, Cato had gained more wealth than Crassus had gained over him. And if even greater riches had come his way, he wouldn't have rejected them. A wise person doesn't think he's unworthy of good fortune. He doesn't love money, but he'd rather have it than not. He doesn't let wealth into his heart, just into his house. He doesn't throw away what he already has. He keeps it and sees it as more material for practicing virtue.

happy-life_section-22.originalText: Who can doubt, however, that the wise man, if he is rich, has a wider field for the development of his powers than if he is poor, seeing that in the latter case the only virtue which he can display is that of neither being perverted nor crushed by his poverty, whereas if he has riches, he will have a wide field for the exhibition of temperance, generosity, laboriousness, methodical arrangement, and grandeur. The wise man will not despise himself, however short of stature he may be, but nevertheless he will wish to be tall: even though he be feeble and one-eyed he may be in good health, yet he would prefer to have bodily strength, and that too, while he knows all the while that he has something which is even more powerful: he will endure illness, and will hope for good health: for some things, though they may be trifles compared with the sum total, and though they may be taken away without destroying the chief good, yet add somewhat to that constant cheerfulness which arises from virtue.
happy-life_section-22.plainEnglish: Who can doubt that a wise man has more opportunities to show his character if he's rich rather than poor? When poor, he can only prove that poverty won't corrupt him or break his spirit. But when rich, he has a wide field to display self-control, generosity, hard work, good planning, and greatness. A wise man won't hate himself for being short, but he'd still prefer to be tall. Even if he's weak and has one eye, he can still be healthy — but he'd rather have a strong body. He knows he has something even more powerful than physical strength. He'll endure sickness and hope for good health. Some things don't matter much compared to what's truly important. You can lose them without losing the most important thing. But they do add something to the steady happiness that comes from virtue.

happy-life_section-22.originalText: Riches encourage and brighten up such a man just as a sailor is delighted at a favourable wind that bears him on his way, or as people feel pleasure at a fine day or at a sunny spot in the cold weather. What wise man, I mean of our school, whose only good is virtue, can deny that even these matters which we call neither good nor bad have in themselves a certain value, and that some of them are preferable to others? to some of them we show a certain amount of respect, and to some a great deal. Do not, then, make any mistake: riches belong to the class of desirable things.
happy-life_section-22.plainEnglish: Wealth cheers up and encourages a wise person, just like a sailor feels joy when a good wind pushes his ship forward, or like people feel happy on a beautiful day or when they find a warm, sunny spot during cold weather. What wise person from our school — where virtue is the only true good — would deny that these things we call "neither good nor bad" still have some value? Some are clearly better than others. We give some of them a little respect, and others a lot of respect. So don't be confused: wealth belongs in the category of desirable things.

happy-life_section-22.originalText: "Why then," say you, "do you laugh at me, since you place them in the same position that I do?" Do you wish to know how different the position is in which we place them? If my riches leave me, they will carry away with them nothing except themselves: you will be bewildered and will seem to be left without yourself if they should pass away from you: with me riches occupy a certain place, but with you they occupy the highest place of all. In fine, my riches belong to me, you belong to your riches.
happy-life_section-22.plainEnglish: "So why are you laughing at me?" you ask. "You put riches in the same place I do." Want to know how different our positions really are? If my wealth leaves me, it takes nothing but itself. You would be lost and confused — you'd feel like you lost yourself if your money disappeared. Wealth has a place in my life, but it has the top place in yours. Here's the key difference: my riches belong to me. You belong to your riches.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: Cease, then, forbidding philosophers to possess money: no one has condemned wisdom to poverty. The philosopher may own ample wealth, but will not own wealth that which has been torn from another, or which is stained with another's blood: his must be obtained without wronging any man, and without its being won by base means; it must be alike honourably come by and honourably spent, and must be such as spite alone could shake its head at. Raise it to whatever figure you please, it will still be an honourable possession, if, while it includes much which every man would like to call his own, there be nothing which any one can say is his own.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish: Stop telling philosophers they shouldn't have money. No one has said that wisdom requires poverty. A philosopher can own plenty of wealth. But it can't be wealth stolen from others or stained with someone else's blood. It must be earned without harming anyone and without using dishonest methods. It must be gained honorably and spent honorably. It should be the kind of wealth that only jealous people would criticize. Make it as large as you want — it will still be an honorable possession. As long as it includes things that everyone would want to own, but nothing that anyone can claim was actually theirs.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: Such a man will not forfeit his right to the favour of Fortune, and will neither boast of his inheritance nor blush for it if it was honourably acquired: yet he will have something to boast of, if he throw his house open, let all his countrymen come among his property, and say, "If any one recognizes here anything belonging to him, let him take it." What a great man, how excellently rich will he be, if after this speech he possesses as much as he had before! I say, then, that if he can safely and confidently submit his accounts to the scrutiny of the people, and no one can find in them any item upon which he can lay hands, such a man may boldly and unconcealedly enjoy his riches.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish: This kind of person won't lose Fortune's favor. He won't brag about his wealth, but he won't be ashamed of it either — as long as he earned it honestly. In fact, he'll have real reason to be proud if he can open his doors to everyone and say, "Look around at everything I own. If anyone sees something that belongs to them, take it." What a great man! How truly rich he would be if he still owned everything after making that offer! So I'm saying this: if someone can confidently let the public examine his finances, and no one can point to anything suspicious, then he can enjoy his wealth openly and without shame.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: The wise man will not allow a single ill-won penny to cross his threshold: yet he will not refuse or close his door against great riches, if they are the gift of fortune and the product of virtue: what reason has he for grudging them good quarters: let them come and be his guests: he will neither brag of them nor hide them away: the one is the part of a silly, the other of a cowardly and paltry spirit, which, as it were, muffles up a good thing in its lap. Neither will he, as I said before, turn them out of his house: for what will he say? will he say, "You are useless," or "I do not know how to use riches?" As he is capable of performing a journey upon his own feet, but yet would prefer to mount a carriage, just so he will be capable of being poor, yet will wish to be rich; he will own wealth, but will view it as an uncertain possession which will some day fly away from him.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish:
A wise man won't let a single dishonest penny into his house. But he won't reject or shut out great wealth if it comes from good fortune and honest work. Why should he begrudge wealth a good home? Let it come and stay with him. He won't brag about it or hide it away. Bragging is foolish, and hiding wealth shows a cowardly, small spirit that hoards good things like a miser.

He won't kick wealth out of his house either. What would he say? "You're useless" or "I don't know how to use money?" He can walk on his own feet, but he'd rather take a carriage if one's available. In the same way, he can handle being poor, but he'd prefer to be rich. He'll own wealth, but he'll see it for what it is — something uncertain that will fly away from him someday.

happy-life_section-23.originalText: He will not allow it to be a burden either to himself or to any one else: he will give it—why do you prick up your ears? why do you open your pockets?—he will give it either to good men or to those whom it may make into good men. He will give it after having taken the utmost pains to choose those who are fittest to receive it, as becomes one who bears in mind that he ought to give an account of what he spends as well as of what he receives. He will give for good and commendable reasons, for a gift ill bestowed counts as a shameful loss: he will have an easily opened pocket, but not one with a hole in it, so that much may be taken out of it, yet nothing may fall out of it.
happy-life_section-23.plainEnglish: He won't let his wealth become a burden to himself or anyone else. He will give it away—why are you getting excited? Why are you reaching for your wallet?—he will give it to good people or to those who might become good because of it. He will take great care to choose the right people to receive it. After all, he knows he should be able to explain how he spends his money just as much as how he earns it. He will give for good and worthy reasons, because a foolish gift is just a shameful waste. His pocket will open easily, but it won't have holes in it. Plenty can be taken out when needed, but nothing will fall out by accident.

happy-life_section-24.originalText: He who believes giving to be an easy matter, is mistaken: it offers very great difficulties, if we bestow our bounty rationally, and do not scatter it impulsively and at random. I do this man a service, I requite a good turn done me by that one: I help this other, because I pity him: this man, again, I teach to be no fit object for poverty to hold down or degrade. I shall not give some men anything, although they are in want, because, even if I do give to them they will still be in want: I shall proffer my bounty to some, and shall forcibly thrust it upon others: I cannot be neglecting my own interests while I am doing this: at no time do I make more people in my debt than when I am giving things away. "What?" say you, "do you give that you may receive again?" At any rate I do not give that I may throw my bounty away: what I give should be so placed that although I cannot ask for its return, yet it may be given back to me. A benefit should be invested in the same manner as a treasure buried deep in the earth, which you would not dig up unless actually obliged.
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: People think giving is easy. They're wrong. It's actually very hard if you want to do it wisely instead of just throwing money around randomly. I help this person because they deserve it. I repay that person because they helped me first. I give to this one out of pity. I teach that one so poverty won't crush their spirit. Some people I won't help at all, even if they're desperate. Why? Because even after I give to them, they'll still be desperate. Some people I'll offer help to. Others I'll force my help on them whether they want it or not. I can't ignore my own needs while I'm doing all this. Strangely, I never have more people owing me favors than when I'm giving things away. You might ask: "So you give just to get something back?" Not exactly. But I don't give just to waste my money either. What I give should be placed where I can't demand it back, but it might come back to me anyway. Think of a gift like treasure buried deep underground. You wouldn't dig it up unless you absolutely had to.

happy-life_section-24.originalText: Why, what opportunities of conferring benefits the mere house of a rich man affords? for who considers generous behaviour due only to those who wear the toga? Nature bids me do good to mankind—what difference does it make whether they be slaves or freemen, free-born or emancipated, whether their freedom be legally acquired or betowed by arrangement among friends? Wherever there is a human being, there is an opportunity for a benefit: consequently, money may be distributed even within one's own threshold, and a field may be found there for the practice of freehandedness, which is not so called because it is our duty towards free men, but because it takes its rise in a free-born mind. In the case of the wise man, this never falls upon base and unworthy recipients, and never becomes so exhausted as not, whenever it finds a worthy object, to flow as if its store was undiminished.
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: Look at the opportunities for kindness that exist in a rich person's household alone. Who says generosity is only for people who wear togas? Nature tells me to help all human beings. What does it matter if they're slaves or free? What does it matter if they were born free or freed later? What does it matter if their freedom came through law or through friendship? Wherever there's a human being, there's a chance to help them. So even within your own home, you can give money away. You can practice generosity right there. We call it generosity not because it's aimed at free people, but because it comes from a free spirit. For a wise person, this kindness never goes to worthless people. And it never runs out. Whenever it finds someone worthy, it flows freely, as if the supply were endless.

happy-life_section-24.originalText: You have, therefore, no grounds for misunderstanding the honourable, brave, and spirited language which you hear from those who are studying wisdom: and first of all observe this, that a student of wisdom is not the same thing as a man who has made himself perfect in wisdom. The former will say to you, "In my talk I express the most admirable sentiments, yet I am still weltering amid countless ills. You must not force me to act up to my rules: at the present time I am forming myself, moulding my character, and striving to rise myself to the height of a great example. If I should ever succeed in carrying out all that I have set myself to accomplish, you may then demand that my words and deeds should correspond,"
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: So you have no reason to misunderstand the noble, brave, and passionate words you hear from people studying philosophy. First, remember this: someone who is learning wisdom is not the same as someone who has already perfected it. The student will tell you, "I say wonderful things, but I'm still struggling with countless problems. Don't expect me to live up to everything I preach. Right now I'm still working on myself, shaping my character, and trying to reach the level of the great examples I follow. If I ever manage to accomplish everything I've set out to do, then you can demand that my actions match my words."

happy-life_section-24.originalText: But he who has reached the summit of human perfection will deal otherwise with you, and will say, "In the first place, you have no business to allow yourself to sit in judgment upon your betters:" I have already obtained one proof of my righteousness in having become an object of dislike to bad men: however, to make you a rational answer, which I grudge to no man, listen to what I declare, and at what price I value all things. Riches, I say, are not a good thing; for if they were, they would make men good: now since that which is found even among bad men cannot be termed good, I do not allow them to be called so: nevertheless I admit that they are desirable and useful and contribute great comforts to our lives.
happy-life_section-24.plainEnglish: But someone who has reached the peak of human excellence will handle you differently. He'll say: "First of all, you have no right to judge people who are better than you. I already have proof that I'm on the right path — bad people hate me. But I'll give you a reasonable answer, which I don't mind giving to anyone. Listen to what I believe and how I value things. I say riches are not good. If they were good, they would make people good. But since you can find wealth even among bad people, it can't be called good. Still, I admit that riches are desirable and useful. They do bring great comfort to our lives."

happy-life_section-25.originalText: Learn, then, since we both agree that they are desirable, what my reason is amongst counting them among good things, and in what respects I should behave differently to you if I possessed them. Place me as master in the house of a very rich man: place me where gold and silver plate is used for the commonest purposes; I shall not think more of myself because of things which even though they are in my house are yet no part of me. Take me away to the wooden bridge[5] and put me down there among the beggars: I shall not despise myself because I am sitting among those who hold out their hands for alms: for what can the lack of a piece of bread matter to one who does not lack the power of dying? Well, then? I prefer the magnificent house to the beggar's bridge.
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: Let me explain, since we both agree these things are worth wanting, why I count them among good things and how I would act differently toward you if I had them. Put me in charge of a very rich man's house. Put me where gold and silver dishes are used for everyday meals. I won't think more of myself because of things that may be in my house but are not part of who I am. Take me away to the wooden bridge and set me down among the beggars. I won't despise myself for sitting with people who hold out their hands for money. What does lacking a piece of bread matter to someone who still has the power to die? So what's my point? I'd prefer the grand house to the beggar's bridge. Put me among beautiful furniture and all the tools of luxury. I won't think myself any happier because my cloak is soft or because my guests lie on purple cushions.

happy-life_section-25.originalText: Place me among magnificent furniture and all the appliances of luxury: I shall not think myself any happier because my cloak is soft, because my guests rest upon purple. Change the scene: I shall be no more miserable if my weary head rests upon a bundle of hay, if I lie upon a cushion from the circus, with all the stuffing on the point of coming out through its patches of threadbare cloth. Well, then? I prefer, as far as my feelings go, to show myself in public dressed in woollen and in robes of office, rather than with naked or half-covered shoulders: I should like every day's business to turn out just as I wish it to do, and new congratulations to be constantly following upon the former ones: yet I will not pride myself upon this: change all this good fortune for its opposite, let my spirit be distracted by losses, grief, various kinds of attacks: let no hour pass without some dispute: I shall not on this account, though beset by the greatest miseries, call myself the most miserable of beings, nor shall I curse any particular day, for I have taken care to have no unlucky days. What, then, is the upshot of all this? it is that I prefer to have to regulate joys than to stifle sorrows.
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: Picture a different scene: I won't be any more miserable if my tired head rests on a bundle of hay instead of lying on a circus cushion with all the stuffing about to burst through its worn, patched fabric. So what's my point? I'd rather show myself in public dressed in fine wool and official robes than with bare or half-covered shoulders. I'd like every day's business to go exactly as I want it to, with fresh congratulations constantly following the last ones. But I won't let this make me proud. Change all this good fortune to its opposite. Let my mind be torn apart by losses, grief, and all kinds of attacks. Let no hour pass without some argument. Even then, surrounded by the worst troubles, I won't call myself the most miserable person alive. I won't curse any particular day, because I've made sure I have no unlucky days. So what's the point of all this? I'd rather have to control my joys than suppress my sorrows.

happy-life_section-25.originalText: The great Socrates would say the same thing to you. "Make me," he would say, "the conqueror of all nations: let the voluptuous car of Bacchus bear me in triumph to Thebes from the rising of the sun: let the kings of the Persians receive laws from me: yet I shall feel myself to be a man at the very moment when all around salute me as a God. Straightway connect this lofty height with a headlong fall into misfortune: let me be placed upon a foreign chariot that I may grace the triumph of a proud and savage conqueror: I will follow another's car with no more humility than I showed when I stood in my own. What then? In spite of all this, I had rather be a conqueror than a captive. I despise the whole dominion of Fortune, but still, if I were given my choice, I would choose its better parts. I shall make whatever befals me become a good thing, but I prefer that what befals me should be comfortable and pleasant and unlikely to cause me annoyance: for you need not suppose that any virtue exists without labour, but some virtues need spurs, while others need the curb."
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: The great Socrates would tell you the same thing. "Make me the conqueror of all nations," he would say. "Let me ride in triumph through Thebes in Bacchus's golden chariot, from east to west. Let Persian kings take orders from me. Even then, I'll still know I'm just a man, even when everyone around me calls me a god. Now connect this great height with a sudden fall into disaster. Put me on some foreign chariot to decorate a cruel conqueror's victory parade. I'll follow behind another man's chariot with no more shame than I showed when I rode in my own. So what? Despite all this, I'd still rather be the conqueror than the prisoner. I despise Fortune's entire kingdom, but if I had to choose, I'd pick the better parts. I'll turn whatever happens to me into something good. But I'd prefer what happens to be comfortable, pleasant, and unlikely to annoy me. Don't think that virtue comes without effort — some virtues need a kick in the pants, while others need to be reined in."

happy-life_section-25.originalText: As we have to check our body on a downward path, and to urge it to climb a steep one; so also the path of some virtues leads down hill, that of others uphill. Can we doubt that patience, courage, constancy, and all the other virtues which have to meet strong opposition, and to trample Fortune under their feet, are climbing, struggling, winning their way up a steep ascent? Why! is it not equally evident that generosity, moderation, and gentleness glide easily downhill? With the latter we must hold in our spirit, lest it run away with us: with the former we must urge and spur it on. We ought, therefore, to apply these energetic, combative virtues to poverty, and to riches those other more thrifty ones which trip lightly along, and merely support their own weight. This being the distinction between them, I would rather have to deal with those which I could practise in comparative quiet, than those of which one can only make trial through blood and sweat. "Wherefore," says the sage, "I do not talk one way and live another: but you do not rightly understand what I say: the sound of my words alone reaches your ears, you do not try to find out their meaning."
happy-life_section-25.plainEnglish: Just as we have to hold back our body when going downhill and push it hard when climbing up, some virtues work the same way. Some virtues lead us downhill, others uphill. Think about it — patience, courage, and persistence all have to fight strong opposition and crush bad luck underfoot. These virtues are clearly climbing, struggling, fighting their way up a steep hill. But what about generosity, moderation, and gentleness? These glide easily downhill. With the gentle virtues, we must hold back our spirit so it doesn't run away with us. With the tough virtues, we must push and drive ourselves forward. So we should use the energetic, fighting virtues when we're poor. When we're rich, we should use the gentler virtues that move lightly and just carry their own weight. Given this difference, I'd rather deal with virtues I can practice in peace than ones I can only try through blood and sweat. "This is why," says the wise man, "I don't say one thing and do another. But you don't really understand what I'm saying. You only hear the sound of my words. You don't try to figure out what they mean."

happy-life_section-26.originalText: "What difference, then, is there between me, who am a fool, and you, who are a wise man?" "All the difference in the world: for riches are slaves in the house of a wise man, but masters in that of a fool. You accustom yourself to them and cling to them as if somebody had promised that they should be yours for ever, but a wise man never thinks so much about poverty as when he is surrounded by riches. No general ever trusts so implicitly in the maintenance of peace as not to make himself ready for a war, which, though it may not actually be waged, has nevertheless been declared; you are rendered over-proud by a fine house, as though it could never be burned or fall down, and your heads are turned by riches as though they were beyond the reach of all dangers and were so great that Fortune has not sufficient strength to swallow them up. You sit idly playing with your wealth and do not foresee the perils in store for it, as savages generally do when besieged, for, not understanding the use of siege artillery, they look on idly at the labours of the besiegers and do not understand the object of the machines which they are putting together at a distance: and this is exactly what happens to you: you go to sleep over your property, and never reflect how many misfortunes loom menacingly around you on all sides, and soon will plunder you of costly spoils, but if one takes away riches from the wise man, one leaves him still in possession of all that is his: for he lives happy in the present, and without fear for the future."
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: "What's the difference between me, a fool, and you, a wise person?" The difference is enormous. Rich people are servants in a wise person's house, but they're masters in a fool's house. You get used to wealth and cling to it as if someone promised it would be yours forever. But a wise person never thinks more about poverty than when surrounded by riches. No general trusts peace so much that he stops preparing for war. Even if war never comes, it's still been declared. You get arrogant about your fine house, as if it could never burn down or collapse. Wealth goes to your head, as if it's beyond all danger and too big for Fortune to destroy. You sit around playing with your money and don't see the dangers coming. You're like barbarians under siege. They don't understand siege weapons, so they watch the enemy work and don't realize what those machines are for. That's exactly what happens to you. You fall asleep over your property and never think about all the disasters waiting to attack you from every side. Soon they'll steal your expensive treasures. But if you take wealth away from a wise person, you still leave him with everything that's truly his. He lives happily in the present and fears nothing about the future.

happy-life_section-26.originalText: "The great Socrates, or any one else who had the same superiority to and power to withstand the things of this life, would say, 'I have no more fixed principle than that of not altering the course of my life to suit your prejudices: you may pour your accustomed talk upon me from all sides: I shall not think that you are abusing me, but that you are merely wailing like poor little babies.'" This is what the man will say who possesses wisdom, whose mind, being free from vices, bids him reproach others, not because he hates them, but in order to improve them: and to this he will add, "Your opinion of me affects me with pain, not for my own sake but for yours, because to hate perfection and to assail virtue is in itself a resignation of all hope of doing well. You do me no harm; neither do men harm the gods when they overthrow their altars: but it is clear that your intention is an evil one and that you will wish to do harm even where you are not able."
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: The great Socrates, or anyone else with the same strength to rise above worldly things, would say: 'I have one firm rule — I will not change how I live to fit your biases. You can pour all your usual complaints on me from every direction. I won't think you're attacking me. You're just crying like little babies.' This is what a wise person would say. His mind is free from vice, so he corrects others — not because he hates them, but to help them improve. And he would add: 'Your opinion of me causes me pain, but not for my sake — for yours. To hate what is good and attack virtue means giving up all hope of doing well yourself. You cannot harm me. People don't harm the gods when they tear down altars either. But your intention is clearly evil, and you want to do damage even when you can't. I put up with your chatter the same way Jupiter puts up with poets' silly stories. One poet gives him wings, another horns. One makes him an adulterer who stays out all night. Another shows him being cruel to the gods or unfair to people. Another makes him seduce noble young men and kidnap them by force — even his own relatives. Another calls him a father-killer who stole someone else's kingdom from his own father.'

happy-life_section-26.originalText: "I bear with your prating in the same spirit in which Jupiter, best and greatest, bears with the idle tales of the poets, one of whom represents him with wings, another with horns, another as an adulterer staying out all night, another is dealing harshly with the gods, another as unjust to men, another as the seducer of noble youths whom he carries off by force, and those, too, his own relatives, another as a parricide and the conqueror of another's kingdom, and that his father's. The only result of such tales is that men feel less shame at committing sin if they believe the gods to be guilty of such actions. But although this conduct of yours does not hurt me, yet, for your own sakes, I advise you, respect virtue: believe those who having long followed her cry aloud that what they follow is a thing of might, and daily appears mightier. Reverence her as you would the gods, and reverence her followers as you would the priests of the gods: and whenever any mention of sacred writings is made, _favete linguis_, favour us with silence: this word is not derived, as most people imagine, from _favour_, but commands silence, that divine service may be performed without being interrupted by any words of evil omen."
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: The only result of such stories is that people feel less ashamed of doing wrong. They think it's okay because the gods supposedly did it too. Even though your behavior doesn't harm me personally, I still want to give you some advice for your own good: respect virtue. Listen to those who have followed virtue for years. They'll tell you it's incredibly powerful — and it gets stronger every day. Treat virtue like you would treat the gods. Respect virtue's followers like you would respect priests. And whenever anyone talks about sacred teachings, _favete linguis_ — give us your respectful silence. Most people think this phrase comes from the word "favor," but it actually means "be quiet." It's a command for silence so divine service can happen without being interrupted by unlucky words. You need this reminder even more. When the oracle speaks, you should listen carefully and quietly. But look what you actually do. When someone shakes a rattle and claims a god told them to do it, you gather around. When some fake holy man cuts his arms and shoulders to make them bleed, you watch. When someone crawls down the street on their knees howling, or when some old man in linen robes comes out during the day carrying a lamp and laurel branch, shouting that a god is angry — you crowd around him and hang on every word. You all feed each other's amazement, declaring that he must be divinely inspired.

happy-life_section-26.originalText: "It is much more necessary that you should be ordered to do this, in order that whenever utterance is made by that oracle, you may listen to it with attention and in silence. Whenever any one beats a sistrum,[6] pretending to do so by divine command, any proficient in grazing his own skin covers his arms and shoulders with blood from light cuts, any one crawls on his knees howling along the street, or any old man clad in linen comes forth in daylight with a lamp and laurel branch and cries out that one of the gods is angry, you crowd round him and listen to his words, and each increases the other's wonderment by declaring him to be divinely inspired."
happy-life_section-26.plainEnglish: You need to be told to do this so that when the real oracle speaks, you'll pay attention and listen quietly. But look what happens instead: whenever someone shakes a rattle and claims a god told them to do it, or when some faker cuts his arms and shoulders to make himself bleed, or when someone crawls down the street on his knees howling, or when some old man in white robes comes out in broad daylight carrying a lamp and a laurel branch, shouting that a god is angry — you all crowd around him. You hang on his every word. You make each other even more amazed by insisting he must be inspired by the gods.

happy-life_section-27.originalText: Behold! from that prison of his, which by entering he cleansed from shame and rendered more honourable than any senate house, Socrates addresses you, saying: "What is this madness of yours? what is this disposition, at war alike with gods and men, which leads you to calumniate virtue and to outrage holiness with malicious accusations? Praise good men, if you are able: if not, pass them by in silence: if indeed you take pleasure in this offensive abusiveness, fall foul of one another: for when you rave against Heaven, I do not say that you commit sacrilege, but you waste your time.
happy-life_section-27.plainEnglish: Look! From his prison cell — which he made more honorable than any government building just by being there — Socrates speaks to you: "What is wrong with you? Why do you attack both gods and people? Why do you slander virtue and insult what is sacred with your nasty accusations? If you can praise good people, do it. If you can't, then stay quiet. If you really enjoy this disgusting abuse, at least attack each other instead. When you rage against Heaven, I won't say you're committing sacrilege — but you're definitely wasting your time."

happy-life_section-27.originalText: I once afforded Aristophanes with the subject of a jest: since then all the crew of comic poets have made me a mark for their envenomed wit: my virtue has been made to shine more brightly by the very blows which have been aimed at it, for it is to its advantage to be brought before the public and exposed to temptation, nor do any people understand its greatness more than those who by their assaults have made trial of its strength. The hardness of flint is known to none so well as to those who strike it. I offer myself to all attacks, like some lonely rock in a shallow sea, which the waves never cease to beat upon from whatever quarter they may come, but which they cannot thereby move from its place nor yet wear away, for however many years they may unceasingly dash against it. Bound upon me, rush upon me, I will overcome you by enduring your onset: whatever strikes against that which is firm and unconquerable merely injures itself by its own violence. Wherefore, seek some soft and yielding object to pierce with your darts.
happy-life_section-27.plainEnglish: I once gave Aristophanes material for a joke. Since then, all the comic poets have made me their target. They've attacked me with their poisonous wit. But their blows have only made my virtue shine brighter. Virtue benefits from being tested in public and exposed to temptation. No one understands how strong virtue is better than those who attack it and test its strength. No one knows how hard flint is better than those who strike it. I stand ready for all attacks, like a lone rock in shallow water. The waves beat against it from every direction but can never move it or wear it away, no matter how many years they crash against it. Attack me, rush at me — I will defeat you by enduring whatever you throw at me. When you strike something firm and unbreakable, you only hurt yourself with your own violence. So go find something soft to pierce with your arrows.

happy-life_section-27.originalText: But have you leisure to peer into other men's evil deeds and to sit in judgment upon anybody? to ask how it is that this philosopher has so roomy a house, or that one so good a dinner? Do you look at other people's pimples while you yourselves are covered with countless ulcers? This is as though one who was eaten up by the mange were to point with scorn at the moles and warts on the bodies of the handsomest men. Reproach Plato with having sought for money, reproach Aristotle with having obtained it, Democritus with having disregarded it, Epicurus with having spent it: cast Phaedrus and Alcibiades in my own teeth, you who reach the height of enjoyment whenever you get an opportunity of imitating our vices! Why do you not rather cast your eyes around yourselves at the ills which tear you to pieces on every side, some attacking you from without, some burning in your own bosoms? However little you know your own place, mankind has not yet come to such a pass that you can have leisure to wag your tongues to the reproach of your betters.
happy-life_section-27.plainEnglish: But do you really have time to spy on other people's wrongdoings and play judge? To ask why this philosopher has such a big house, or why that one eats so well? You're looking at other people's pimples while you're covered with countless sores. It's like someone with a terrible rash pointing and laughing at the moles and freckles on beautiful people. Go ahead — criticize Plato for wanting money, Aristotle for getting it, Democritus for ignoring it, Epicurus for spending it. Throw Phaedrus and Alcibiades in my face too, you who get your biggest thrill from copying our worst habits! Why don't you look around at your own problems instead? They're tearing you apart from every direction — some attacking from outside, others burning inside your chest. No matter how little you understand your own situation, humanity hasn't sunk so low that you have time to waste badmouthing your betters.

happy-life_section-28.originalText:
This you do not understand, and you bear a countenance which
does not befit your condition, like many men who sit in the circus
or the theatre without having learned that their home is already
in mourning: but I, looking forward from a lofty standpoint, can
see what storms are either threatening you, and will burst in
torrents upon you somewhat later, or are close upon you and on the
point of sweeping away all that you possess. Why, though you are
hardly aware of it, is there not a whirling hurricane at this moment
spinning round and confusing your minds, making them seek and avoid
the very same things, now raising them aloft and now dashing them
below? . . . . . .”


[1] Lipsius’s conjecture, “those who are dressed in white as well
as those who are dressed in coloured clothes,’ alluding to the white
robes of candidates for office, seems reasonable.

[2] The Latin words are literally “to divide” their vote, that is,
“to separate things of different kinds comprised in a single vote
so that they might be voted for separately.”—Andrews.
happy-life_section-28.plainEnglish: You don't realize this. Your face shows you have no idea what's really happening to you. You're like people sitting in the circus or theater who don't know their house is already on fire. But I can see from up high what storms are coming your way. They will either hit you soon in torrents, or they're already close and about to sweep away everything you have. Even though you barely notice it, isn't there a spinning hurricane right now whirling around your mind? It makes you want and avoid the same things. One moment it lifts you up, the next it slams you down.

happy-life_section-28.originalText:
Séneque fait allusion ici à une coutume pratiquée dans les assemblées
du Sénat; et il nous I’explique lui-même ailleurs d’un manière très
claire: “Si quelqu’un dans le Sénat,” dit il, “ouvre un avis, dont
une partie me convienne, je le somme de la detacher du reste, et
j’y adhère.”—_Ep_. 21, La Grange.

[3] _Parentatur_ seems to mean where an offering is made to luxury—
where they sacrifice to luxury. Perfumes were used at funerals.
Lipsius suggests that these feasts were like funerals because the
guests were carried away from them dead drunk.

[4] The quotation is from the epitaph on Phaeton.—See _Ovid_, Met.
II, 327.

[5] The “Pons Sublicius,” or “pile bridge,” was built over the Tiber
by Ancus Martius, one of the early kings of Rome, and was always
kept in repair out of a superstitious feeling.

[6] _Sistrum_. A metallic rattle used by the Egyptians in celebrating
the rites of Isis, &c.—Andrews.

happy-life_section-28.plainEnglish: This appears to be editorial footnotes and commentary rather than a passage from Seneca's "On the Happy Life" itself. These are scholarly annotations explaining references in Seneca's text, including Latin phrases, historical context, and literary allusions. This is not a passage that can be translated as it's already explanatory material written by editors or translators.
